title: From Stateless Nightmares to Durable Agents — Samuel Colvin, Pydantic

primary.label: Orchestration & Durable Execution
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is durable execution for AI agent workflows using Temporal, covering crash recovery, retries, checkpoints, and replay of cached activities. PydanticAI is developer tooling for building agents, while the deep research demo is a general-purpose application pattern. The talk addresses making AI agent workflows survive failures in production and long-running deployments. The content assumes understanding of agent architectures, workflow engines, and Python async programming. This is a recorded conference talk with live code demonstrations. Claims are directly stated in the transcript with supporting excerpts.

summary:
Samuel Colvin introduces PydanticAI's support for durable execution frameworks, currently Temporal and Deboss, with more being added via pull requests. He frames the core problem: stateless LLM applications work fine for simple demos but become painful at scale when long-running workflows fail, losing compute, progress, and user trust. He notes OpenAI publicly uses Temporal for Deep Research, and other LLM providers do similar things.

The first demo is a 20 Questions game with two PydanticAI agents: an answer agent (Haiku 3.5) and a questioner agent that calls a tool to ask questions. This toy example is directly analogous to deep research, where an agent sequentially queries external sources. Without durable execution, a crash forces a full restart.

Colvin wraps the agents in Temporal agent wrappers, creating durable versions with minimal code changes. Temporal's architecture requires deterministic workflows and non-deterministic activities (IO, including LLM calls and tool calls). PydanticAI's Temporal integration automatically converts LLM calls and tool calls into activities. Colvin criticizes OpenAI's own Temporal support for not handling tool calls as activities, calling it a 'chocolate teapot.' He demos failure injection and process killing, showing Temporal replays cached activity results in milliseconds without re-calling the LLM.

Colvin then presents a deep research implementation with three agent types: a plan agent (structured data extraction returning a research plan), parallel search agents (using Gemini Flash or Tavily), and an analysis agent (Claude Sonnet 4.5). He argues agents are now the 'quantum of development'—micro-tasks composed into larger autonomous systems. The workflow uses plain imperative Python with task groups for parallelism; Temporal handles parallelism and snapshotting without special code. A Vertex SDK bug forced switching to OpenAI responses with Tavily for the durable version.

He demonstrates the durable deep research workflow surviving a process kill: on restart, the plan step replayed in 24 milliseconds, searches returned instantly from Temporal's cache, and only the unfinished analysis activity re-ran. The system produced a report recommending PydanticAI with Temporal. Colvin also shows Pydantic Evals comparing GPT 4.1, Gemini, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 on the 20 Questions task, noting Gemini appeared faster but was actually inventing wrong answers—a cautionary tale about evaluation rigor. He briefly announces the upcoming Pydantic AI Gateway for inference and observability.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Stateless LLM architectures work for demos but fail painfully at scale—crashes lose all compute, progress, and user trust
Temporal records every activity's inputs and outputs, enabling deterministic workflow replay and resume-from-checkpoint
PydanticAI's Temporal integration wraps agents so LLM calls and tool calls become activities automatically with minimal code changes
Temporal replays cached activity results in milliseconds without re-calling the LLM, resuming from the exact failure point
Deep research can be built as composed micro-agents: plan, parallel search, and analysis—using plain imperative Python with task groups for parallelism
Temporal handles parallelism and long-running activities natively; workflows can even sleep for days and Temporal pauses everything
Evals can be misleading: Gemini appeared faster on 20 Questions but was inventing wrong answers, highlighting the need for rigorous evaluation
Durable execution provides more granular snapshotting than graphs for workflows that aren't complex enough to need graph structures
OpenAI's own Temporal support lacks tool-call activity support, which Colvin calls effectively useless ('a chocolate teapot')
Pydantic AI Gateway is upcoming for inference from major models, open source models, and self-hosting with observability

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation for Durable Execution
sections.summary: Colvin introduces PydanticAI's support for Temporal and Deboss durable execution frameworks, explains why stateless architectures fail at scale for long-running workflows, and mentions OpenAI uses Temporal for Deep Research.

sections.title: 20 Questions Demo Without Durable Execution
sections.summary: A toy 20 Questions demo with two PydanticAI agents (answer agent on Haiku 3.5, questioner agent) illustrates the problem: if the process dies, execution restarts from scratch. Colvin notes this is structurally equivalent to deep research.

sections.title: Converting to Durable Temporal Agents
sections.summary: Colvin wraps agents in Temporal agent wrappers, explains Temporal's workflow/activity model (deterministic workflows, non-deterministic activities for IO), and critiques OpenAI's Temporal support for lacking tool-call activities.

sections.title: Live Demo: Failure Injection and Automatic Retry
sections.summary: Colvin runs the Temporal workflow with injected failures (20% then 10%), showing automatic retry. The demo experiences slowdowns, requiring a Temporal server restart.

sections.title: Live Demo: Process Kill and Resume from Checkpoint
sections.summary: Colvin kills the running process to simulate Kubernetes termination, then resumes the workflow via its workflow ID. Temporal replays cached activity results in milliseconds without re-calling the LLM, resuming from the exact failure point. Logfire shows full traces. Colvin mentions running Pydantic Evals on different models.

sections.title: Pydantic Evals Results and Model Comparison
sections.summary: Colvin shows eval results comparing GPT 4.1, Gemini, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 on 20 Questions. Gemini appeared cheaper and faster, but he discovered it was inventing wrong answers, illustrating the importance of rigorous evaluation. One run was still failing after 46 steps trying to guess 'potato.'

sections.title: Deep Research Implementation Without Durability
sections.summary: Colvin presents a deep research system with three composed agents: a plan agent (structured data extraction), parallel search agents (Gemini Flash with Tavily), and an analysis agent (Claude Sonnet 4.5). He argues agents are now the 'quantum of development'—micro-tasks composed into autonomous systems. The workflow uses plain imperative Python with task groups for parallelism. He demos it running in Logfire with full observability.

sections.title: Durable Deep Research with Temporal
sections.summary: Colvin shows the durable version wrapping agents in Temporal. A Vertex SDK bug forced switching to OpenAI responses with Tavily. The analysis agent gets a 1-hour timeout. The workflow code remains identical—plain imperative Python with task groups. Colvin notes you could sleep for days inside a workflow and Temporal handles pausing. He kicks off a query about the best Python agent framework for durable execution and type safety.

sections.title: Durable Deep Research: Crash Recovery Demo and Results
sections.summary: The durable deep research workflow survives a process kill. On restart, the plan step replayed in 24ms, searches returned instantly from Temporal's cache, and only the unfinished analysis activity re-ran. The system produced a report recommending PydanticAI with Temporal. Colvin notes UI work is still needed for a proper deep research interface.

sections.title: Announcements and Closing
sections.summary: Colvin mentions the durable execution code will be merged to the public repo, shares a QR code, and announces the upcoming Pydantic AI Gateway for inference from major and open source models with observability and enterprise self-hosting. He closes with thanks and QR codes for learning more.
